Abstract

Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io.
1 Introduction

World models (WM) [1, 2, 3] have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied decisionmaking [4, 5, 6, 7]. By learning predictive models of environment dynamics, they enable testtime reasoning and the synthesis of novel behaviors for unseen goals by searching in the action space [8, 9, 10, 11]. However, planning with WMs faces two fundamental challenges: 1) search complexity grows exponentially with planning horizon, and 2) prediction errors accumulate over long rollouts. Therefore, most WM-based planners are restricted to short-horizon tasks [8, 9], rely on simplified action abstractions [10], or operate in high-level spaces such as language, sacrificing fine-grained control [12].

Hierarchical learning offers a principled solution to this scalability challenge by decomposing longhorizon problems into manageable abstractions [13, 14, 15]. It has been extensively studied in Reinforcement Learning (RL) [16, 17, 18, 19], where hierarchy mitigates the credit assignment problem in long trajectories, and in imitation learning [20, 21], where it enables reusable behaviors. More recently, hierarchical structure has been introduced into diffusion-based planners to avoid directly modeling entire trajectories [22, 23, 24], improving scalability and generalization beyond fixed-horizon training data.
How can we enable the same capabilities for task-agnostic world models, enabling long-horizon zeroshot planning for unseen goals? A direct approach would be to simply increase the prediction horizon

or action abstraction (e.g., frame-skipping) [25]. However, previous attempts at hierarchical world models typically depend on task-specific priors to function effectively, relying on pre-trained skills and low-level policies [19, 26] or rewards and value functions to verify subgoal feasibility [27, 28]. This dependency arises because planning is fundamentally adversarial: without these anchoring constraints, a powerful optimizer will inevitably exploit deficiencies in a learned world model, discovering "wormholes" or unrealistic transitions [29, 30]. To make hierarchical world models suitable for planning, we must construct a latent space that both condenses trajectory information to minimize search complexity, and remains inherently well-behaved to prevent the planner from exploiting unrealistic transitions.

To this end, we introduce ID-WM, a hierarchical world model with implicit dynamics grounded in the insight that effective planning requires decoupling topological reachability from execution details (Figure 1). ID-WM consists of a high-level diffusion-based world model that only implicitly models the dynamics by outputting states that are within a fixed distance away from the current state, functioning as a neighboring state generator, and a deterministic low-level model conditioned on both current state and action, acting as an inverse dynamics solver. Conditioned on the current state and a Gaussian noise, the high-level model leverages the generative power of diffusion to map a tractable unit Gaussian latent space to the manifold of feasible neighboring states. This formulation allows us to treat the noise as an implicit high-level action, enabling the planner to search over a well-behaved distribution instead of complex, discontinuous skill spaces to reason purely about "where to go," while the low-level model recovers the precise executable actions for "how to get there."
We summarize our contributions as follows:

• We introduce ID-WM, a hierarchical world model that decouples reachability from control, eliminating the need for task-specific value functions or pre-trained policies. • We propose a corresponding hierarchical planning algorithm that bridges high-level abstraction with local dynamics, enabling robust, long-horizon decision-making. • Across three navigation and manipulation environment suites, ID-WM shows 38.5% improvement for reaching arbitrary goals against powerful hierarchical offline reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and diffusion planning methods, and crucially, a 135% improvement over single-level world model and planning regimes.
2 Related Work
2.1 Hierarchical Learning
Hierarchical learning has long been a foundational pursuit in artificial intelligence, decomposing long-horizon problems into manageable abstractions [13, 14, 15]. This paradigm spans policy

architectures [31], reinforcement learning [16, 18, 27, 32], imitation learning [20], and planning [28, 33]. Existing work focuses on both behavioral (skills/options) [14, 19, 26, 34, 35, 36, 37] and subgoal-centric approaches [17, 28, 38]. However, these methods typically rely on coupled priors, such as rewards, learned value functions or pre-trained low-level policies [28, 32] to ensure feasibility, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. In contrast, we eliminate this dependency, enabling robust hierarchical reasoning purely through implicit dynamics even when reliable value functions and policies are absent.
2.2 World Models for Embodied Planning

World models [1, 2, 3] have emerged as a foundational paradigm for embodied decision-making, enabling agents to reason about the future consequences of their actions. Recently, the field has shifted towards developing general-purpose world models [5, 8, 10, 39, 40, 41] capable of capturing broad environmental dynamics, diverging from traditional model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) where learning task-specific reward or value functions is paramount [42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48]. Once these dynamics are learned, inference-time planning algorithms like the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) [49] or gradient descent—are employed to derive behaviors zero-shot [8, 9, 11, 50]. However, the effectiveness of these approaches is often constrained to short horizons due to the computational complexity of search and the accumulation of prediction errors over time. While various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these issues, ranging from robust gradient-based optimization [30, 51] and efficient sampling routines [52] to temporal approximations for longer action sequences [10], they remain fundamentally flat in their temporal reasoning. Consequently, they struggle with longhorizon task solving, remaining susceptible to local minima and limited in their scalability to complex behaviors. Concurrently, HWM [25] builds a hierarchical latent world model by increasing the high-level frameskip and learning macro-actions; in contrast, ID-WM searches over the diffusion noise space, which is smooth and well-conditioned by construction.
2.3 Diffusion Models and Planning

Diffusion probabilistic models [53, 54, 55] excel at capturing complex, multimodal distributions via iterative denoising. Their efficacy is proven across high-dimensional modalities, including pixels [40, 41, 56, 57], language [58], and robot actions [59, 60]. Recently, diffusion models have been proposed as zero-shot planners for embodied tasks [61, 62, 63, 64]. These methods model entire trajectories directly, limiting generalization to out-of-distribution initial-goal pairs and constraining planning horizons to those seen during training. While hierarchical formulations mitigate these constraints, they rely on task-specific value functions [22, 23, 32], successful task trajectories [65], or assumed access to low-level primitives [24]. In contrast, we redefine diffusion as a local generator rather than a global planner. By delegating long-horizon reasoning to search, our method composes local jumps into novel trajectories without requiring task-specific priors.
3 Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics

Overview and Problem Formulation. We consider a goal-conditioned planning problem within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple M = (S, A, P), where S is the continuous state space, A is the action space, and P(st+1|s≤t, a≤t) represents the transition dynamics.

Following prior world modeling methods [8, 10, 11], we learn environment dynamics from a taskagnostic offline dataset without any reward labeling via a world model, and plan to reach arbitrary unseen goals at test time. More specifically, an agent is provided with an initial state o0 and a goal state og at test time. The objective is to execute a sequence of actions (a0, a1, . . . , aT −1) such that the distance between the agent’s final state oT and the goal og is minimized. Unlike prior work, we do not assume a fixed task horizon T [8], focusing instead on enabling the agent to perform autonomous long-horizon reasoning and planning.

Implicit High-Level Action Space. A key insight of our approach is to treat the initial noise vector zt as an implicit high-level action. Unlike discrete skill indices or learned latent codes which may suffer from mode collapse or topological discontinuities, illustrated in Section 6.13, the noise space Z = Rd is inherently smooth and well-behaved (isotropic Gaussian). By optimizing over zt, the planner searches over the standard Gaussian latent space, where any sample z maps to a physically valid reachable state on the data manifold via the deterministic DDIM mapping.

4 Experiments
Our experiments are designed to answer the following key questions:
• Subgoal Generation: Can ID-WM reliably generate diverse and feasible reachable states?
• Generalization: Can ID-WM solve long-horizon planning tasks to reach arbitrary, zeroshot goals at test time?
• Scaling: How does the performance of ID-WM scale across environments of increasing complexity?
• Visual Planning: Is ID-WM effective for long-horizon planning directly from highdimensional visual observations?
4.1 Environments

We evaluate ID-WM on three navigation and manipulation environment suites as shown in Figure 3. The environments are Wall, PushT, and Maze, with task horizon ranging from hundreds to thousands of environment steps. A full description of the environments is detailed in Section 6.1.

4.2 Baselines

We compare ID-WM with five state-of-the-art offline learning methods including imitation learning (GCBC), offline RL (HIQL), diffusion planners (Diffuser, Hierarchical Diffuser), and planning with world models (Single-level WM with MPC). See Section 6.4 for full details.
4.3 Generating Neighboring States with ID-WM

We first investigate the extent to which each level of ID-WM accurately captures the underlying data distribution and predicts future states across varying temporal granularities. Specifically, for the high-level WM, we evaluate whether sampling from the latent prior yields diverse and reachable future states.

In Figure 4, we sample 100 latent noise vectors z ∼N(0, I) and visualize the resulting generated states ˆs∆= fhi(s0, z, ∆) reachable within a ∆-step horizon. For each ∆, we overlay all 100 generated samples to visualize the predicted state distribution, explicitly marking the agent’s position with a black dot for clarity.

As illustrated in Figure 4, the high-level WM generates diverse and physically reachable states for both the Wall and PushT environments. In the Wall environment, the dispersion of agent positions increases with ∆, reflecting a larger reachable radius as the temporal budget grows. Similarly, in the PushT environment, we observe an increasingly diffused distribution of both the agent and the T-block. The smooth coverage of object configurations demonstrates that the model successfully captures the complex, multi-modal interactions between the agent and the object. This high-fidelity distribution modeling serves as a necessary prerequisite for planning, enabling the system to generate diverse trajectories and generalize effectively to unseen goals in downstream tasks.
Figure 4: Diverse neighboring states generated with the high-level WM of ID-WM.
4.4 Hierarchical Planning with ID-WM
Can ID-WM solve long-horizon planning tasks to reach arbitrary, zero-shot goals at test time? To this end, we conduct hierarchical planning on three environment suites.

For all environments and baselines, we randomly sample 50 pairs of initial and goal states, with sampling method detailed in Section 6.2, and report the average performance across these instances. For the PushT task, we report two metrics: the success rate and the final coverage of the T-block relative to the target configuration. A trial is considered successful only if both the agent and the T-block reach their respective goal positions. In contrast, the final coverage metric provides a more granular measure of performance by focusing specifically on the object’s alignment. To further evaluate generalization capabilities, we test PushT under two settings: a standard regime and a data-augmented regime featuring random spatial transformations and rotations. All experiments are conducted with a maximum horizon of 2000 environment steps. For all experiments, ID-WM uses ∆= 5 (25 environment steps with frameskip) and Hhi = 5 subgoals per high-level plan, without
per-task tuning; the planner replans after each executed plan (up to 15 replans), so no prior knowledge of the goal distance is required. We ablate ∆and the number of subgoals in Section 6.7.

In Table 1, ID-WM outperforms all baselines, achieving a 38.5% overall improvement and 135% gain over single-level WM with MPC (SL-WM). The gap is most evident in PushT with random goals, where ID-WM is the only approach exceeding a 30% success rate without augmentation. While SL-WM performs well on shorter horizons (Maze, Wall), it fails on PushT’s long-horizon requirements (often > 100 steps) due to exponential search complexity and compounding prediction errors. Furthermore, the remaining baselines exhibit distinct failure modes. GCBC performs well on indistribution goals (e.g., fixed-goal PushT) and in environments with dense data coverage (Medium Maze, Wall) but degrades significantly on out-of-distribution (OOD) goals. HIQL shows potential for OOD generalization but demands dense data coverage to accurately learn value functions, reflected in its performance gap between PushT and PushT-Aug. While H-Diffuser offers marginal improvements, it still relies heavily on dense data. Even with data augmentation (Section 6.3), H-Diffuser’s success rate remains low, primarily because it struggles to jointly attend to both the object and the agent’s final position.

4.5 How does ID-WM scale with task complexity?
We investigate whether ID-WM scales to tasks of increasing complexity across two dimensions: environment size and goal horizon.

Scaling with Maze Size. We evaluate ID-WM across four mazes of increasing difficulty: U-Maze (3 × 3), Medium Maze (6 × 6), Large Maze (7 × 10), and Giant Maze (13 × 13) (Figure 7a). Each dataset contains 2,000 random 100-step trajectories. Given a fixed dataset size, data coverage naturally becomes sparser as maze size increases.

While all methods achieve near-perfect success on the U-Maze, baselines degrade significantly in larger environments (Figure 7a). In contrast, ID-WM maintains the highest performance on the Large Maze. We hypothesize this is because ID-WM combines local dynamics modeling with high-level planning, effectively "stitching" together regions of sparse data. Unlike GCBC or Diffuser (which model entire trajectories simultaneously) or HIQL (which requires dense data for global value functions), ID-WM does not rely on global trajectory coverage. Furthermore, while H-Diffuser uses abstraction, it lacks an explicit dynamics model, resulting in brittle plans requiring expensive,
high-frequency replanning. By grounding its hierarchy in explicit local dynamics, ID-WM generates robust, scalable plans.

Scaling with Goal Horizon. Building on the PushT planning benchmark introduced by Zhou et al. [8] (which evaluates goals 25 steps away), we increase complexity by sampling goals from the validation set that are d ∈{25, 50, . . . , 150} steps away.

We compare ID-WM against a single-level world model baseline that performs full-horizon CEM search and replanning at every step. While the total number of executed actions is identical, ID-WM achieves a near-perfect success rate across all horizons as shown in Figure 7b). This confirms our main PushT results (Table 1), demonstrating that ID-WM maintains precise goal-reaching capabilities even when goals are over 150 steps away.
4.6 Vision-based Planning with ID-WM

To evaluate ID-WM in high-dimensional observation spaces, we test it on a vision-based PushT task. We use the state-based PushT dataset augmented with four 90◦rotations for spatial robustness. Observations (3 × 64 × 64 images) are encoded into 4 × 8 × 8 latents using a pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE [66]. We compare against AVDC [64], a language-conditioned video planner that generates all subgoals simultaneously (details in Section 6.4).

As shown in Figure 8, ID-WM generates reliable, sequential subgoals that ensure steady progress. In contrast, AVDC fails to produce meaningful plans, likely because the initial-goal pairs are out-ofdistribution. This highlights the generalization advantage of iterative subgoal search over simultaneous generation—which relies heavily on trajectory-level dataset coverage—even within compressed visual spaces.

We compare against two additional baselines: DINO-WM [8], a flat single-level world model planner, and HWM [25], a concurrent hierarchical latent world model that uses a larger frameskip for its high-level model. In this setting, ID-WM uses DINO-WM as its low-level world model, so the comparison between DINO-WM and ID-WM isolates the gain provided by the hierarchy. ID-WM achieves the best performance on the most challenging long-horizon settings (d = 50, d = 75, and Random Goal), demonstrating its effectiveness for long-horizon vision-based planning.

5 Conclusion

We present ID-WM, a hierarchical world modeling and planning framework that decouples temporally extended subgoal generation from local reachability. By treating diffusion noise as implicit actions, we constrain the planning search space to a unit Gaussian, ensuring reliable subgoal generation. ID-WM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and demonstrates high-quality vision-based subgoal generation. Ultimately, grounding hierarchical abstraction in explicit local dynamics represents a promising step toward robust, long-horizon decision-making.

Limitations. First, ID-WM’s reliance on search-based optimization within a diffusion latent space incurs higher inference times than reactive policies or deterministic world models. Future work will explore amortized or gradient-based planning to mitigate this bottleneck. Second, while our hierarchy prevents planning complexity from scaling with trajectory length, it still scales with state-space dimensionality. Integrating compact, structured representation learning could further streamline this planning process for highly complex environments.
